varieties.name: Sun Gold
varieties.notes: Orange cherry with exceptional sweetness; early and prolific. Splits after heavy rain, so water evenly.

varieties.name: Juliet
varieties.notes: Grape-shaped mini-Roma that resists cracking and holds on the vine; very productive and tolerant of rough conditions.

varieties.name: Early Girl
varieties.notes: Reliable early slicer; a good pick where summers are short or cool, and quick to fill a gap between heat waves.

varieties.name: Stupice
varieties.notes: Czech heirloom that sets fruit in cool weather; small, tangy slicers where summers are short or nights stay chilly.

varieties.name: Glacier
varieties.notes: Compact semi-determinate that ripens small red fruit very early; one of the best for cool, short northern seasons.

varieties.name: Celebrity
varieties.notes: All-America winner with a broad disease package; dependable medium-large slicers in almost any climate.

varieties.name: Better Boy
varieties.notes: Big, heavy crops of classic red slicers and good disease resistance; forgiving of imperfect care.

varieties.name: Heatmaster
varieties.notes: Bred to keep setting fruit when days and nights stay hot; a top choice for the Deep South and desert Southwest.

varieties.name: Solar Fire
varieties.notes: Florida-bred heat-set tomato; keeps producing crack-resistant medium-large fruit through hot, humid summers.

varieties.name: Cherokee Purple
varieties.notes: Dusky purple-brown heirloom with deep, smoky-sweet flavor; less disease resistance than hybrids.

varieties.name: Brandywine
varieties.notes: Pink potato-leaf beefsteak famous for flavor; low yields and sets poorly in extreme heat, so give it a long mild season.

varieties.name: Black Krim
varieties.notes: Dark brick-red Russian heirloom with rich, slightly salty flavor; copes with summer heat better than most beefsteaks.

varieties.name: San Marzano
varieties.notes: Long Italian sauce tomato, meaty with few seeds; ripens over a long window rather than all at once.

varieties.name: Roma
varieties.notes: Determinate paste tomato that ripens a concentrated crop, which makes it easy to can or sauce in one batch.

varieties.name: California Wonder
varieties.notes: The standard blocky bell, green ripening to red; thick walls for stuffing. Best with a long warm season.

varieties.name: King of the North
varieties.notes: Open-pollinated bell bred for northern gardens; ripens red reliably where summers are short or cool.

varieties.name: Big Bertha
varieties.notes: Very large, elongated thick-walled bells and heavy yields; the pick for oversized stuffing peppers.

varieties.name: Gypsy
varieties.notes: All-America winner; wedge-shaped yellow-to-red sweet peppers very early and in quantity, even in cooler summers.

varieties.name: Corno di Toro
varieties.notes: Long curved Italian 'bull's horn' in red or yellow; the classic sweet pepper for roasting and grilling.

varieties.name: Sweet Banana
varieties.notes: Long pale-yellow sweet pepper ripening to red; mild, prolific, and tolerant of cooler weather than bells.

varieties.name: Shishito
varieties.notes: Thin-walled Japanese pepper picked green and blistered; mostly mild with the odd hot one. Wildly prolific.

varieties.name: Jalapeño
varieties.notes: The classic garden chile with moderate heat; pick green, or let ripen red for sweeter, hotter fruit and chipotle.

varieties.name: Serrano
varieties.notes: Small thin-walled chile, hotter than jalapeño and crisp raw in salsas; very productive in hot weather.

varieties.name: Cayenne
varieties.notes: Long, slender, hot pods that dry easily for flakes and powder; a reliable producer in most climates.

varieties.name: Hungarian Hot Wax
varieties.notes: Waxy yellow 'hot banana' with mild-to-moderate heat; sets well in cool summers and great for pickling.

varieties.name: Poblano
varieties.notes: Wide, mild stuffing chile for rellenos; dried red it becomes ancho. Needs a long warm season to ripen red.

varieties.name: Anaheim
varieties.notes: Long, mild green chile for roasting and peeling; dries red for ristras. Thrives in hot, dry climates.

varieties.name: Habanero
varieties.notes: Very hot lantern pods with a fruity aroma; slow, so start early or grow in a pot where summers are short.

varieties.name: Scotch Bonnet
varieties.notes: Caribbean habanero relative, just as hot but sweeter and fruitier; the jerk chile. Wants a long, hot season.

varieties.name: Ghost Pepper (Bhut Jolokia)
varieties.notes: Superhot (around 1 million SHU) and very slow; best in hot climates or started early and grown in a large pot.

varieties.name: Black Beauty
varieties.notes: Classic large glossy-purple globe; needs a long, hot summer to produce well.

varieties.name: Ichiban
varieties.notes: Long, slender Japanese type; thin-skinned, tender and productive, and earlier than big globe varieties.

varieties.name: Hansel
varieties.notes: All-America winner; clusters of finger-size purple fruit on compact plants. A top pick for short seasons and pots.

varieties.name: Fairy Tale
varieties.notes: Small purple-and-white striped fruit, sweet with few seeds, on a dwarf plant; very early and good in containers.

varieties.name: Ping Tung Long
varieties.notes: Long lavender Taiwanese heirloom; tender skin, sweet flesh, and among the most heat- and disease-tolerant eggplants.

varieties.name: Listada de Gandia
varieties.notes: Purple-and-white striped Italian heirloom with mild, rich flesh; sets well in hot weather.

varieties.name: Rosa Bianca
varieties.notes: Round lavender-and-white Italian heirloom; creamy, mild and not bitter. The cook's globe eggplant.

varieties.name: Casper
varieties.notes: Pure-white slender fruit with mild, mushroom-like flesh; pick before the skin toughens.

varieties.name: Provider
varieties.notes: Germinates in cool soil better than most; early, dependable and the go-to bush snap where springs are cold.

varieties.name: Contender
varieties.notes: Early bush snap that keeps setting in heat better than most; stringless if picked young.

varieties.name: Blue Lake Bush 274
varieties.notes: Classic round, stringless snap with a concentrated set; great for canning and freezing in one picking.

varieties.name: Royal Burgundy
varieties.notes: Purple pods (turn green when cooked) on plants that tolerate cool soil; easy to spot at picking time.

varieties.name: Dragon Tongue
varieties.notes: Flat cream pods streaked purple; tender as a snap bean and good as a shelling bean if left to fill.

varieties.name: Kentucky Wonder
varieties.notes: Old-time pole bean with rich flavor; needs a trellis and picks over a long season.

varieties.name: Blue Lake Pole
varieties.notes: Pole version of the classic Blue Lake; months of stringless pods from one trellis where seasons are long.

varieties.name: Rattlesnake
varieties.notes: Purple-streaked pole snap that keeps producing in hot, humid summers when other beans drop their blossoms.

varieties.name: Marketmore 76
varieties.notes: Dark-green slicer with broad disease resistance; the dependable standard in most climates.

varieties.name: Straight Eight
varieties.notes: Old All-America slicer with uniform 8 in. fruit; reliable almost anywhere.

varieties.name: Diva
varieties.notes: Thin-skinned, seedless, never bitter; sets fruit without pollinators, so ideal under row cover or in a greenhouse.

varieties.name: Spacemaster
varieties.notes: Short-vined bush slicer for containers and small beds; full-size fruit on a compact plant.

varieties.name: National Pickling
varieties.notes: Blocky, blunt-ended pickler bred for even brining; pick small for gherkins or larger for spears.

varieties.name: Suyo Long
varieties.notes: Ribbed Chinese burpless type to 15 in.; sweet, heat-tolerant and stays non-bitter when stressed. Trellis it.

varieties.name: Armenian
varieties.notes: Long, pale, ribbed fruit (botanically a melon); thrives in hot, dry summers and is never bitter.

varieties.name: Lemon
varieties.notes: Round yellow heirloom, mild and crisp; very productive and pick before it turns deep yellow.

varieties.name: Black Beauty
varieties.notes: Classic dark-green bush zucchini; productive and widely available.

varieties.name: Dunja
varieties.notes: Open, spineless plant with strong powdery-mildew and virus resistance; keeps producing longer into late summer.

varieties.name: Costata Romanesco
varieties.notes: Ribbed Italian heirloom with superb nutty flavor and edible blossoms; big plant, lower yield.

varieties.name: Eight Ball
varieties.notes: All-America winner; round dark-green fruit picked at baseball size for stuffing. Compact plant.

varieties.name: Early Prolific Straightneck
varieties.notes: Smooth pale-yellow straightneck on an early bush plant; easier to wash and slice than a crookneck.

varieties.name: Yellow Crookneck
varieties.notes: Bumpy-skinned Southern heirloom with a curved neck; buttery flavor, best picked under 6 in.

varieties.name: Zephyr
varieties.notes: Slender yellow fruit with a pale-green tip; firm, nutty flesh that holds up on the grill.

varieties.name: Tromboncino
varieties.notes: Climbing Italian moschata with long curved fruit; resists squash vine borer, so a good choice where borers are bad.

varieties.name: Table Queen
varieties.notes: The classic ribbed dark-green acorn; one fruit halves into two servings. Quick enough for short seasons.

varieties.name: Honey Bear
varieties.notes: All-America winner on a compact semi-bush plant with powdery-mildew tolerance; small, sweet single-serving fruit.

varieties.name: Delicata
varieties.notes: Cream-and-green striped fruit with thin edible skin and sweet, nutty flesh; roast without peeling.

varieties.name: Waltham Butternut
varieties.notes: The benchmark butternut: long solid neck, small seed cavity, keeps for months and resists squash vine borer.

varieties.name: Honeynut
varieties.notes: Mini butternut, sweeter and denser than Waltham; ripens tan to deep orange. Full-size vine, single-serving fruit.

varieties.name: Sunshine
varieties.notes: All-America winner; scarlet kabocha with smooth, sweet, stringless flesh that tastes good right after curing.

varieties.name: Vegetable Spaghetti
varieties.notes: The original spaghetti squash; pale-yellow oblong fruit whose flesh pulls into strands when cooked.

varieties.name: Tivoli
varieties.notes: All-America winner; bush-habit spaghetti squash that fits a small bed or large container.

varieties.name: Jack Be Little
varieties.notes: Palm-size ribbed orange minis for decorating; many fruit per vine and edible when roasted.

varieties.name: Sugar Pie
varieties.notes: Small, sweet pumpkin with thick, dry flesh; the one to grow for baking rather than carving.

varieties.name: Long Island Cheese
varieties.notes: Flat, buff, cheese-wheel heirloom with smooth sweet flesh for pies; stores for months.

varieties.name: Connecticut Field
varieties.notes: The traditional American jack-o'-lantern pumpkin; large, smooth orange fruit on long vines.

varieties.name: Howden
varieties.notes: The jack-o'-lantern standard: big, tall, ribbed, uniform fruit with sturdy handle stems.

varieties.name: Rouge Vif d'Etampes
varieties.notes: The flattened red-orange 'Cinderella' pumpkin; striking decoration and good for soups.

varieties.name: Atlantic Giant
varieties.notes: The variety behind record-setting giants; needs huge space, rich soil, steady water and a long season.

varieties.name: Scarlet Nantes
varieties.notes: Cylindrical, blunt-tipped, sweet and nearly coreless; the benchmark for fresh eating.

varieties.name: Bolero
varieties.notes: Nantes hybrid with leaf-blight resistance and excellent storage; a top pick for fall and overwintered crops.

varieties.name: Danvers 126
varieties.notes: Tapered, strong-topped carrot that copes with heavier soil and heat better than most.

varieties.name: Chantenay Red Cored
varieties.notes: Short, broad-shouldered roots for heavy or shallow soil and deep containers; stores well.

varieties.name: Imperator 58
varieties.notes: Long, tapered supermarket shape; needs deep, loose, stone-free soil to size up.

varieties.name: Little Finger
varieties.notes: True baby carrot, 3–4 in. long; quick, sweet, and suited to containers and shallow soil.

varieties.name: Paris Market
varieties.notes: Golf-ball-round roots that handle heavy, rocky or shallow soil; good in containers.

varieties.name: Cosmic Purple
varieties.notes: Purple skin over an orange core; sweet and colorful, best raw or lightly cooked.

varieties.name: Black-Seeded Simpson
varieties.notes: Fast, light-green leaf lettuce; the classic early cut-and-come-again crop.

varieties.name: Red Sails
varieties.notes: All-America winner; bronze-red ruffled leaves that are slow to bolt and slow to turn bitter.

varieties.name: Buttercrunch
varieties.notes: All-America butterhead with thick, tender leaves; holds longer in warm weather than most bibbs.

varieties.name: Parris Island Cos
varieties.notes: Standard tall green romaine; crisp, upright, and tolerant of mosaic virus and tipburn.

varieties.name: Jericho
varieties.notes: Romaine bred in Israel's desert heat; stays sweet and slow to bolt when other lettuces turn bitter.

varieties.name: Nevada
varieties.notes: Batavian with crunchy, juicy leaves; strongly resistant to bolting and tipburn in summer heat.

varieties.name: Little Gem
varieties.notes: Miniature romaine, crisp and sweet; fast and tight-spaced, so it fits between cool spells and heat waves.

varieties.name: Winter Density
varieties.notes: Compact romaine-bibb cross that tolerates frost; good for fall, overwintering and early spring sowings.

varieties.name: Lacinato
varieties.notes: Dark blistered strap leaves (dinosaur kale); sweet, holds texture when cooked, and tolerates warm weather well.

varieties.name: Red Russian
varieties.notes: Flat oak-like leaves with purple stems; tender and mild enough for salads, and very frost-hardy.

varieties.name: Winterbor
varieties.notes: Tall, heavily curled blue-green kale; one of the most cold-hardy, for harvest well into winter.

varieties.name: Dwarf Blue Curled
varieties.notes: Low, compact curly kale (often sold as Vates) for small beds and containers; overwinters in many areas.

varieties.name: Redbor
varieties.notes: Deep purple, tightly curled hybrid; as ornamental as it is edible, and sweetens after frost.

varieties.name: Siberian
varieties.notes: Broad, frilly blue-green leaves on a tough plant; extremely winter-hardy and a strong overwintering kale.

varieties.name: Portuguese (Tronchuda)
varieties.notes: Smooth, cabbage-like leaves with thick white ribs; the caldo verde green, and copes with heat better than most.

varieties.name: Texas Early Grano 502
varieties.notes: Sweet, mild yellow short-day onion, the parent of the 1015Y; plant in fall or late winter in the South.

varieties.name: Yellow Granex
varieties.notes: The Vidalia-type sweet onion: flat, very mild bulbs for short-day regions. A poor keeper, so eat fresh.

varieties.name: Red Creole
varieties.notes: Firm, pungent red short-day onion that thrives in hot climates; the best keeper of the short-day group.

varieties.name: Red Burgundy
varieties.notes: Mild red short-day onion with red-ringed flesh; good raw in salads. Not a long keeper.

varieties.name: Candy
varieties.notes: Sweet, jumbo yellow onion that bulbs across most of the country; the safest pick if unsure of day length.

varieties.name: Walla Walla
varieties.notes: Famous jumbo sweet onion for northern gardens; long-day, so it won't bulb in the South. Eat fresh, not a keeper.

varieties.name: Yellow Sweet Spanish
varieties.notes: Large, mild long-day globe for the North; keeps moderately well and is widely sold as plants and seed.

varieties.name: Evergreen Hardy White
varieties.notes: Perennial clumping bunching onion that survives hard winters and divides itself; cut and it keeps coming.

varieties.name: Tokyo Long White
varieties.notes: Long, thick white shanks for grilling and cooking; hill soil around stems to blanch them longer.

varieties.name: White Lisbon
varieties.notes: Fast, classic seed-rack scallion with mild white stems; sow every few weeks for a steady supply.

varieties.name: Parade
varieties.notes: Uniform, upright non-bulbing scallion for tidy bunches; holds without swelling if left in the ground.

varieties.name: Deep Purple
varieties.notes: Purple-red shanks that keep their color raw; same easy culture as the white types.

varieties.name: California Early
varieties.notes: Mild artichoke softneck that needs little winter chill; a dependable default for mild-winter regions.

varieties.name: Inchelium Red
varieties.notes: Large, mild artichoke softneck that stores well; widely adapted from cold to fairly mild winters.

varieties.name: Silverskin
varieties.notes: Longest-storing garlic (up to a year) and the classic braiding type; strong flavor and suited to mild winters.

varieties.name: Music
varieties.notes: Porcelain hardneck with big cloves and scapes; needs real winter cold and is unreliable where winters are mild.

varieties.name: German Extra Hardy
varieties.notes: Very winter-hardy porcelain with few, large, strong-flavored cloves; a top choice for the coldest zones.

varieties.name: Chesnok Red
varieties.notes: Purple-stripe hardneck that keeps its rich flavor when baked; best where winters are cold.

varieties.name: Creole Red
varieties.notes: Low-chill Creole with rose-purple cloves and excellent storage; one of the best for the South and Southwest.

varieties.name: Elephant Garlic
varieties.notes: A leek relative, not true garlic: huge, very mild cloves. Undemanding about winter chill.

varieties.name: Dark Red Norland
varieties.notes: Early red-skinned, white-fleshed potato; great for new potatoes and short northern seasons.

varieties.name: Yukon Gold
varieties.notes: All-purpose buttery yellow flesh; early-mid season, good for new potatoes and stores well.

varieties.name: Red LaSoda
varieties.notes: Red potato bred for the South; the most reliable red for a warm-climate spring crop.

varieties.name: Red Pontiac
varieties.notes: Vigorous red-skinned potato that adapts to many soils and stores well; good in containers.

varieties.name: Kennebec
varieties.notes: Big white all-purpose tubers, disease-tolerant and forgiving; excellent for fries and chips.

varieties.name: All Blue
varieties.notes: Blue skin and flesh that holds color when cooked; moist texture best for salads and roasting.

varieties.name: Russian Banana
varieties.notes: Yellow fingerling with firm, waxy flesh; superb roasted or in salads, not for mashing.

varieties.name: Russet Burbank
varieties.notes: The classic late baking potato with floury flesh; needs a long season and even moisture to size up.

varieties.name: Cherry Belle
varieties.notes: Round bright-red salad radish; fast, mild and crisp. The classic quick crop.

varieties.name: French Breakfast
varieties.notes: Oblong red radish with a white tip; mild and tender. Pick promptly, as it turns pithy fast in warm weather.

varieties.name: Champion
varieties.notes: Larger round red radish that stays crisp and mild past the size where smaller types go pithy.

varieties.name: White Icicle
varieties.notes: Long white tapered root; crisp, slightly hotter, and holds a little better into warm weather.

varieties.name: Watermelon
varieties.notes: Green-skinned with bright pink flesh; mild and sweet. Best sown for a fall crop in cooling weather.

varieties.name: Minowase
varieties.notes: Long white Japanese daikon for pickling and braising; sow in late summer, as it bolts in warming spring weather.

varieties.name: Black Spanish Round
varieties.notes: Black-skinned, white-fleshed winter radish; pungent and stores for months. Sow for fall.

varieties.name: Rat-Tail
varieties.notes: Grown for crisp, spicy edible seed pods rather than roots; thrives in summer heat that ruins other radishes.

varieties.name: Bloomsdale Long Standing
varieties.notes: Crinkled dark-green savoy; the classic, and slower to bolt than most open-pollinated spinach.

varieties.name: Winter Bloomsdale
varieties.notes: Very cold-hardy savoy for fall sowing and overwintering under mulch; gives an early spring crop.

varieties.name: Space
varieties.notes: Smooth-leaf hybrid; fast, upright and easy to wash, with downy-mildew resistance. Good for baby leaf.

varieties.name: Tyee
varieties.notes: Upright semi-savoy with strong bolt resistance; the safest pick for a late spring sowing.

varieties.name: New Zealand Spinach
varieties.notes: Not a true spinach, but crops all summer when real spinach bolts; the practical hot-season stand-in.

varieties.name: Malabar Spinach
varieties.notes: Climbing tropical vine with thick, succulent leaves that thrives in heat; best cooked in stir-fries and soups.

varieties.name: Sugar Snap
varieties.notes: All-America winner; plump, sweet edible pods eaten whole. Tall climber that needs a 6 ft trellis.

varieties.name: Sugar Ann
varieties.notes: Dwarf 2 ft snap pea and the earliest of all; needs little or no support, so it suits containers.

varieties.name: Oregon Sugar Pod II
varieties.notes: Flat, tender snow-pea pods on semi-dwarf vines; resists powdery mildew and enation virus.

varieties.name: Mammoth Melting Sugar
varieties.notes: Large, tender snow pods on tall vines; the classic stir-fry pea and more forgiving of warm spells than most.

varieties.name: Green Arrow
varieties.notes: Heavy-yielding English shelling pea with slim pods of 8–11 peas, mostly in pairs; easy to pick.

varieties.name: Little Marvel
varieties.notes: Compact, early dwarf shelling pea with sweet peas; needs little support.

varieties.name: Wando
varieties.notes: Tolerates both cold and early heat better than other shelling peas; good for late spring or fall sowings.

varieties.name: Tom Thumb
varieties.notes: Tiny 8–9 in. heirloom for pots and window boxes; frost-tolerant and genuinely productive.

varieties.name: Calypso
varieties.notes: One of the slowest-bolting cilantros, with compact, leafy plants; best for stretching harvest into warm weather.

varieties.name: Santo
varieties.notes: Widely available slow-bolting standard; leafy and dependable for spring and fall sowings.

varieties.name: Leisure
varieties.notes: Slow-bolting with lush, finely cut leaves; a reliable choice for repeated cuttings.

varieties.name: Cruiser
varieties.notes: Upright, thick-stemmed and uniform plants that are easy to cut in bunches; slow to bolt.

varieties.name: Bouquet
varieties.notes: Classic pickling dill with big early flower heads; quick to leaf, but grow it mainly for seed and heads.

varieties.name: Fernleaf
varieties.notes: All-America winner; compact 18 in. plants slow to bolt. The best dill for containers and leaf harvest.

varieties.name: Mammoth Long Island
varieties.notes: Tall 4–5 ft heirloom grown for heavy seed heads; the traditional dill-pickle variety.

varieties.name: Dukat
varieties.notes: Sweet, extra-leafy dill that holds its foliage longer before flowering; good for repeated leaf cuts.

varieties.name: Italian Flat Leaf
varieties.notes: The cooking parsley: stronger flavor and easier to chop than curly. The default choice.

varieties.name: Giant of Italy
varieties.notes: Tall, thick-stemmed flat-leaf with the biggest leaves and heaviest yield per plant.

varieties.name: Moss Curled
varieties.notes: Tightly ruffled garnish parsley; sturdy, frost-tolerant and tidy in borders and containers.

varieties.name: Forest Green
varieties.notes: Vigorous dark curly type on long stems that stays presentable through a long cutting season.

varieties.name: Hamburg Rooted
varieties.notes: Grown for its parsnip-like white root as much as its leaves; a winter soup vegetable. Direct-sow only.

varieties.name: Genovese
varieties.notes: Classic large-leaf Italian pesto basil; susceptible to downy mildew in humid summers.

varieties.name: Prospera
varieties.notes: Genovese-type bred for downy-mildew resistance; the pick where basil collapses to mildew in humid late summer.

varieties.name: Italian Large Leaf
varieties.notes: Big, soft leaves, sweeter and less clove-like than Genovese; the other standard pesto basil.

varieties.name: Sweet Thai
varieties.notes: Anise-scented leaves on purple stems; holds up in heat and is slower to go woody than sweet basil.

varieties.name: Mrs. Burns' Lemon
varieties.notes: Intensely lemon-scented basil from the Southwest; vigorous in heat. Great for fish, salads and tea.

varieties.name: Dark Opal
varieties.notes: Deep purple leaves with a milder, clove-like flavor; colors vinegars and oils and doubles as an ornamental.

varieties.name: Cinnamon
varieties.notes: Spicy cinnamon scent over sweet basil, with purple stems and flowers; good in fruit salads and desserts.

varieties.name: Holy Basil (Tulsi)
varieties.notes: A different species: musky, peppery and clove-heavy; the basil for tea and pad kra pao. Thrives in heat.

varieties.name: Tuscan Blue
varieties.notes: Fast, tall upright rosemary with broad, flavorful leaves on straight stems; the best for cooking and skewers.

varieties.name: Arp
varieties.notes: One of the most cold-hardy rosemaries, with an open, gray-green habit; the pick where winters are borderline.

varieties.name: Madeline Hill
varieties.notes: Also sold as 'Hill Hardy'; good flavor and among the hardiest rosemaries for overwintering in the ground.

varieties.name: Blue Spires
varieties.notes: Dense, very upright plant with heavy blue bloom; makes a tidy edible hedge in mild climates.

varieties.name: Prostrate
varieties.notes: Trailing form that spills over walls, raised beds and pots; milder flavor and less cold-hardy than uprights.

varieties.name: English Thyme
varieties.notes: Broad-leaf kitchen standard; sturdy, productive and the easiest for cutting sprigs.

varieties.name: French Thyme
varieties.notes: Narrow gray leaves, sweeter and more refined than English; slightly less cold-hardy. The bouquet-garni thyme.

varieties.name: German Winter
varieties.notes: The toughest culinary thyme: dense, very winter-hardy and quick to rebound after a hard cut.

varieties.name: Lemon Thyme
varieties.notes: True lemon scent over thyme, great with chicken and fish; variegated forms are common and just as usable.

varieties.name: Creeping Thyme
varieties.notes: Flat, flowering mat for paths and between stepping stones; edible but mild. Grow for groundcover, not the kitchen.

varieties.name: Spearmint
varieties.notes: The cooking and mojito mint: sweet with low menthol. If a recipe just says 'mint', this is it.

varieties.name: Peppermint
varieties.notes: Sharp, cooling menthol; the tea and candy mint, usually too strong for savory dishes.

varieties.name: Kentucky Colonel
varieties.notes: Large-leaved, heavy-yielding spearmint; the classic julep mint and easy to pick by the handful.

varieties.name: Moroccan
varieties.notes: Upright spearmint with clean, intensely sweet flavor; the classic for mint tea.

varieties.name: Chocolate Mint
varieties.notes: Peppermint with a cocoa-like note and dark stems; good in desserts and after-dinner tea.

varieties.name: Apple Mint
varieties.notes: Fuzzy round leaves with a soft fruity flavor and little menthol; handles heat and part shade well.
